title: Data Visualization
text:
Exercises
Use mtcars to show the relationship between car weight (wt) and fuel economy (mpg). Make the plot deliberately ugly while keeping it technically valid.
::: {callout-tip collapse=“true”}

Example solution

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg,colour = factor(cyl), 
                   shape = factor(gear), size = hp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("magenta", "yellow", "cyan")) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 20)) +
  labs(title = "AN EXTREMELY IMPORTANT CAR GRAPH",
       x = "Weight",
       y = "MILES PER GALLON",
       colour = "CYLINDERS",
       shape = "GEARS",
       size = "HORSEPOWER")








:::






Resources




Fundamentals of Data Visualization Claus O. Wilke

title: Data frames
text:
A data frame is a rectangular collection of vectors of equal length. Each column is a vector (a variable). Each row is an observation. Different columns can contain different types of data.

# create one
travellers <- data.frame(
  name = c("Arthur", "Ford", "Trillian", "Zaphod"),
  planet = c("Earth", "Betelgeuse", "Earth", "Betelgeuse"),
  age = c(30, 200, 30, NA),
  towels = c(1, 2, 1, 0), 
  knows_answer = c(NA, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))


travellers

1   Arthur      Earth  30      1           NA
2     Ford Betelgeuse 200      2         TRUE
3 Trillian      Earth  30      1         TRUE
4   Zaphod Betelgeuse  NA      0        FALSE

# look at the top rows
head(travellers, 2)

title: R as a calculator
text:
Maths: + - * / ^

3 + 1 - 2

[1] 2

(3 + 4) / 2

[1] 3.5

3^2

[1] 9

# Division 
15 / 6

[1] 2.5

15 %/% 6 # integer part

[1] 2

15 %% 6 # remainder

[1] 3





Assign: <- =

1x <- 3
y = 3 


1

Note: In R, both <- and = can be used to assign a value to an object. <-is the conventional assignment operator in R. You will often see = used inside function calls to specify arguments. Keeping these two uses separate can make code easier to read.




Comparison: == != < > <= >=

y == x 

[1] TRUE

x == 6

[1] FALSE

y != x 

[1] FALSE


Logical: & and |

(x < 5) & (y == 5)

[1] FALSE

(x < 5) | (y == 5)

[1] TRUE







vectors
data frames (and tibbles)
matrices (and arrays)
lists





one-dimensional collection of values

Common vector types/classes:

logical: TRUE / FALSE
numeric: a vector that contains numbers
character: a vector that contains strings of text


logical_vector   <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
numeric_vector   <- c(4, 5.2, pi)
character_vector <- c("four", "five", "six")

More info see: r-bloggers

# c() creates a vector
1v <- c(4, "four", 1+pi)

# [ ] lets you subset from the vector 
v[3]


1

Atomic vectors can only contain one type. So adding a character to your vector makes all the values characters (coercion)




[1] "4.14159265358979"








Note




v_character <- c("four", 1+pi, 1.5+exp(1), 'almost four')# "" vs '' is preference
is.character(v_character)

[1] TRUE

class(v_character) 

[1] "character"

typeof(v_character) 

[1] "character"



v_numeric <- c(4, 1+pi, 1.5+exp(1))
is.numeric(v_numeric)

[1] TRUE

class(v_numeric) # high-level data structure - user's perspective

[1] "numeric"

typeof(v_numeric) # internal representation

[1] "double"


returns “double” because by default numeric values are stored as “double-precision numbers”

title: 0HM120 Advanced data analysis
0HM120 Advanced data analysis
Practicalities
text:
An R script is a plain text file that contains R code. R scripts use the file extension .R.
You can run:

a single line of code
several selected lines
the entire script

Comments start with #. R ignores anything after # on that line.
Comments are useful for explaining what your code does or leaving notes for yourself.



A notebook (Rmarkdown .Rmd or Quarto .qmd) is a file that can contain both normal text and executable R code.
Unlike an R script, a notebook can combine:

explanatory text
R code
output
tables
figures
equations

R code is placed inside code chunks
When you run the chunk, the output can appear directly underneath the code.
This makes notebooks particularly useful for data analysis because you can keep the code, results, and explanation together in one document.




R comes with many built-in functions, but you can add more functionality using packages.


A package only needs to be installed once:
install.packages("tidyverse")



A package needs to be loaded each time you start a new R session:
library(tidyverse)




Functions perform actions in R. You have already used functions such as c().
A function is usually followed by parentheses:

mean(c(1, 2, 3))

[1] 2


Values supplied to a function are called arguments:

round(3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14


Packages provide additional functions. For example, after loading ggplot2 from tidyverse, you can use functions provided by that package.



Some simple habits make your R code much easier to read:

use meaningful object names
add spaces around operators
use comments where they are useful
keep your formatting consistent

See: R-bloggers

title: Probability and statistics
text:
The following uses Pishro-Nik (2014)


A random experiment is a procedure where uncertain events are observed. An outcome is the result of such an experiment, and the collection of all possible outcomes is called the sample space \(S\). For example:

a coin toss: \(S = \{heads,tails\}\)
roll a 6 sided die (D6): \(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\)
number of rainy days in June: \(S = \{0, 1, ..., 30\}\)

Repetitions of a random experiment is known as a trial. If a coin is tossed twice \(S = \{(H, H), (T, H), (H, T), (T, T)\}\).
An event is a subset of the sample space.
The numerical results of an a random experiment are random variables(RV). For the example of a coin tossed twice, numeral values can be assigned to each outcome: \((H, H) = 0, (T, H) = 1, ...\)

title: Working with data
text:
R has a set of descriptive statistics functions.



Function
Description




table(x)
Counts how often each value occurs


sum(x)
Adds the values


mean(x)
Arithmetic mean


median(x)
Median


var(x)
Variance


sd(x)
Standard deviation


min(x)
Minimum


max(x)
Maximum


range(x)
Returns the minimum and maximum




# Example
marks <- c(7.5, 9, NA, 8, 6.5, 8, 7.5)
round(sd(marks, na.rm = TRUE), 3)

[1] 0.822

range(marks, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 6.5 9.0








Missing values



Many functions return NA when the data contain missing values because the functions have na.rm = TRUE by default. Use na.rm = TRUE when you want the calculation to ignore missing values.

mean(marks)

[1] NA

mean(marks, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 7.75





table(marks)

marks
6.5 7.5   8   9 
  1   2   2   1 








Note



table() does not show missing values by default. If you want to see them, try:

table(marks, useNA = "ifany")

marks
 6.5  7.5    8    9 <NA> 
   1    2    2    1    1 







The built-in iris data frame contains measurements for 150 iris flowers. You can inspect its help page with ?iris.


How many variables does iris contain? What are their names?


















Hint 1





Two useful functions are ncol() and names().











Fully worked solution






ncol(iris)

[1] 5

names(iris)

[1] "Sepal.Length" "Sepal.Width"  "Petal.Length" "Petal.Width"  "Species"     









Create a frequency table showing how many flowers belong to each species.















Hint 1





Use the Species column.











Hint 2





Use $ to select a column from a data frame











Fully worked solution






table(iris$Species, useNA = "ifany")


    setosa versicolor  virginica 
        50         50         50 









Compute the mean, median, and range of Petal.Length.















Hint 1





You need the functions mean(), median(), and range().











Hint 2





Select petal length with: iris$Petal.Length











Fully worked solution






mean(iris$Petal.Length)

[1] 3.758

median(iris$Petal.Length)

[1] 4.35

range(iris$Petal.Length)

[1] 1.0 6.9

title: Getting started
text:
Free and open source
Designed for statistics and data analysis

For most cases the base statistical modelling and data-visualisation libraries

Modular: extend it with thousands of specialist packages
Encourages transparent, reproducible code rather than hidden “button-clicking”
Combines analysis, figures, citations, and writing in reproducible reports\

Why R rather than Python?
Python is an excellent general-purpose language, while R was developed specifically for statistical computing and graphics. This does not mean that R is always better than Python. Python is often preferable for software development, machine learning systems, etc.
Used in practice

The BBC published an R cookbook and the bbplot package for creating reproducible, publication-ready graphics in its house style.
Quarto can turn an analysis into journal-ready HTML, PDF, or Word manuscripts, with journal-specific templates available through extensions.

title: Getting started
text:
Actually starting
After installing both R and RStudio, open RStudio, in the Console type:

print("Hello world")
3 + 2
?mean

Make a new file:

In the menu File > New File > Rscript
Type 40 + 2 in the newly created script, then click Ctrl+Enter
Alternatively: select 40 + 2 and click on ‘Run’
To save the R script: File > Save / Save as.
